newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection begins in NYC bank case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection begins in NYC bank case.

text.p: Jury selection began on Tuesday in a bank fraud case against Cuban-born banker Orlando Castro Llanes, his son and his grandson.
Most of the 80 jurors questioned by Manhattan State Supreme Court Judge Edward McLaughlin said it would be difficult for them to serve on the case because it could last three or four months.

The three men are accused of illegally using deposits in a family-controlled bank, Banco Progreso International de Puerto Rico (BPIPR), to prop up financial institutions they controlled in Central and South America.
BPIPR closed down in January 1995 with uninsured losses to depositors of more than $15 million, prosecutors said.
The case is being tried here because prosecutors claim money in the alleged frauds was transferred through New York banks, including two multimillion dollar transfers.
One prospective juror, a young woman, got into a shouting match with the judge and was near tears when he would not excuse her.
"The thought of such a lengthy trial being held during the holiday season is not exactly what is on the jurors' wish list for this year," said Richard Sharpstein, attorney for the eldest Castro.
He said he expected a jury could be sworn in by next week.

Castro, known as "Don Orlando," his son Orlando Castro Castro, and his grandson, Jorge Castro Barredo, are charged with scheming to defraud, and the two younger men also face grand larceny charges. They have pleaded not guilty.
U.S. prosecutors claim the three misled Venezuelan depositors to believe BPIPR was a safe off-shore bank subject to tight regulatory control, attracting deposits of more than $55 million.

Castro, a Cuban exile accused of playing a key role in Venezuela's 1994 banking crisis, left Venezuela that year after arrest warrants were issued for him and several associates on charges of financial fraud and other crimes.
All three men have been in jail since they were arrested in April in Florida. The Venezuelan government has begun extradition proceedings.
